task_3.title: Fix template arithmetic operator precedence
task_3.description: Template expressions now evaluate mixed arithmetic using standard operator precedence and same-level left-to-right associativity, correcting previously incorrect render results for combinations of addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division, and modulo.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that arithmetic expressions in templates produce the mathematically expected result when combining addition, subtraction, multiplication, division, floor division, modulo, and comparisons in a single expression.

expectation.grounded: Jinja template expression parsing must treat `+` and `-` as the same precedence level, and `*`, `/`, `//`, and `%` as the same higher precedence level, with operations within each level evaluated left to right. Comparison parsing, including `in` and `not in`, must consume operands using the corrected arithmetic precedence so the compared values reflect the intended math result.
expectation.conceptual: Mixed math in template expressions should behave like normal arithmetic: multiplicative operators are resolved before additive operators, operators at the same level are evaluated from left to right, and any comparison should use those corrected numeric results.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve existing public expression features outside this precedence fix, including concatenation with `~`, exponentiation handling, and comparison operators. It must not require users to add parentheses for standard arithmetic precedence to work correctly.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should only correct arithmetic interpretation errors without changing unrelated expression capabilities or forcing template authors to rewrite ordinary math expressions.

behavior: Expressions that mix `+` and `-` now evaluate those operators at the same precedence level instead of giving one of them unintended priority.
Expressions that mix `*`, `/`, `//`, and `%` now evaluate those operators at the same precedence level instead of nesting them with unintended priority.
Multiplicative operations are evaluated before additive operations in mixed arithmetic expressions.
Operators within the same arithmetic precedence level are associated left to right.
Comparison expressions, including membership checks with `in` and `not in`, now compare values produced by the corrected arithmetic precedence rules.
acceptance_criteria: When a template expression combines multiplication or modulo with addition or subtraction, it should render the result produced by standard arithmetic precedence.
When a template expression combines multiple additive operators, it should evaluate them left to right.
When a template expression combines multiple multiplicative operators such as division, floor division, modulo, or multiplication, it should evaluate them left to right within that precedence level.
When a comparison or membership expression uses arithmetic on either side, it should compare the fully evaluated arithmetic value rather than a value derived from incorrect operator grouping.
When existing templates use arithmetic expressions that already rely on standard precedence, they should no longer need extra parentheses to obtain the expected result.

task_1.title: Scope template cache entries to the active loader
task_1.description: Jinja 2.9 changes how Environment template cache entries are identified so cache lookups stay fast and remain tied to the current loader instance. This fixes the 2.8 performance regression and prevents stale templates from being reused when the loader changes but the template name stays the same.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `Environment` template caching remains performant and returns the correct template for the currently configured loader, including when loaders do not expose file-backed sources and when the loader is replaced at runtime.

expectation.grounded: With caching enabled, `Environment.get_template(name)` should scope cached templates to the active loader instance and the template name, rather than deriving cache identity from `loader.get_source()` results or source paths. Repeated requests for the same name from the same loader should still reuse the cached template subject to existing cache size and reload rules, while changing `Environment.loader` should cause later lookups of the same name to resolve against the new loader instead of reusing a template cached under the previous loader.
expectation.conceptual: Template caching should be keyed by which loader is serving the template, not by a resolved file path. After upgrading, applications should see the same fast cache reuse for repeated lookups from one loader, and they should get fresh content when the environment switches to a different loader that serves the same template name.

constraints.grounded: Do not regress existing cache controls: disabled caching must still avoid template reuse, bounded caches must still evict entries according to their configured size, and cached templates must still honor the environment's reload behavior before reuse. The cache identity change must not require source-path support from loaders.
constraints.conceptual: Keep current caching behavior intact aside from the cache identity fix. Cache disablement, cache size limits, and reload checks should continue to behave as before, and loaders should not need filesystem-style metadata in order to participate in caching.

behavior: `Environment.get_template(name)` reuses cached templates only when both the loader instance and template name match the original lookup.
Cache lookup no longer depends on resolving a source path through `loader.get_source()` only to identify the cache entry.

If `Environment.loader` is replaced with a different loader that provides the same template name, a later lookup of that name resolves and caches the template from the new loader instead of returning the previous loader's cached template.
Loaders without file-backed source paths can still participate in caching for repeated template lookups.
acceptance_criteria: When an `Environment` with caching enabled loads the same template name multiple times from the same loader without requiring reload, it should reuse the cached template instance.

When an `Environment` swaps from one loader to another loader that serves the same template name, the next lookup of that template name should return the template from the new loader rather than stale content from the old loader.
When a loader does not provide a usable file-backed source path, repeated template lookups with caching enabled should still work without depending on source-path-derived cache identity.
When caching is disabled or size-limited, the existing no-cache and eviction behavior should remain unchanged while using the new cache identity semantics.

task_2.title: Enable generator-stop semantics in compiled templates
task_2.description: The upgrade adds support for Python's generator-stop behavior in generated template code on interpreters that support it. This makes template execution surface unintended StopIteration escapes as runtime failures instead of allowing generator termination behavior to end rendering implicitly, while keeping older Python versions compatible.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates compiled and rendered on supported Python versions use generator-stop semantics so unexpected StopIteration raised by application code during template execution is surfaced as an error instead of silently terminating template generation.

expectation.grounded: Templates compiled through the normal Jinja2 code-generation path should enable the Python future feature `generator_stop` when the interpreter supports it, alongside existing future features already used for generated templates. On Python 3.5 and later, rendering through public template APIs such as `Template.render` and environment-based compilation should therefore convert a leaked `StopIteration` from user-invoked code into the runtime error associated with generator-stop handling. On interpreters that do not support `generator_stop`, template compilation must remain valid and continue without that future feature.
expectation.conceptual: On Python runtimes that support generator-stop behavior, template rendering should no longer treat an unexpected StopIteration from application code as a normal end of template generation. Instead, rendering should fail clearly with the runtime error Python uses for that situation, while older runtimes continue to render templates without requiring unsupported syntax.

constraints.grounded: Support for `generator_stop` must be conditional on interpreter support and must not introduce syntax errors on older supported Python versions. Existing template compilation behavior unrelated to generator-stop, including other active future features and ordinary successful rendering, should remain unchanged.
constraints.conceptual: The change must preserve compatibility with older Python versions and avoid altering normal template output when no unexpected StopIteration is raised.

behavior: On Python 3.5 and later, generated template code opts into `generator_stop` semantics during compilation.

If application code reached from a template expression, call, filter, or attribute access raises `StopIteration` during rendering on a supported runtime, template execution raises the runtime error produced by generator-stop handling instead of ending generation implicitly.
On Python versions that do not support `generator_stop`, templates continue to compile and run without enabling that future feature.
acceptance_criteria: Given Python 3.5 or later and a template that invokes application code which raises StopIteration during rendering, when the template is rendered, it should fail with a runtime error rather than finishing normally or truncating output silently.
Given Python 3.5 or later and a template that does not trigger StopIteration, when it is compiled and rendered, it should behave the same as before apart from the enabled generator-stop semantics.

Given a supported Python runtime that lacks `generator_stop`, when templates are compiled and rendered through standard Jinja2 APIs, they should continue to work without unsupported future-import syntax.

task_4.title: Add opt-in async template execution support
task_4.description: Version 2.9 adds an opt-in async mode for template execution. In this mode, templates can consume async iterables and awaitable results, expose async rendering and module APIs, and keep synchronous entry points usable where possible, while enforcing explicit async-mode boundaries.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates support an opt-in async execution mode so applications can render against async iterables and awaitable helpers on supported Python runtimes, while keeping async-only limitations explicit and predictable.

expectation.grounded: Applications must be able to enable async behavior through `Environment(..., enable_async=True)` or `Template(..., enable_async=True)`. In async mode, `Template.render_async()` must provide coroutine-based rendering, `Template.generate_async()` must provide async streaming, and `Template.make_module_async()` must provide async module creation. Template evaluation in async mode must accept async iterables in `for` loops, await awaitable results produced by template calls and async-aware built-in filters, and allow includes, imports, macros, and blocks to execute under async rendering. `render()` and `generate()` should still produce rendered output when async mode is enabled. `Template.module` must be unavailable in async mode, and loop length access for async iterators without a known length must fail instead of returning a guessed value.
expectation.conceptual: When async mode is enabled, users should be able to render templates against asynchronous data sources and awaitable helper results using normal template syntax. The library should offer explicit async APIs for full rendering, streaming, and module creation, while preserving synchronous rendering entry points where feasible. Async mode should also expose clear failure behavior for capabilities that cannot be represented safely in synchronous form.

constraints.grounded: Behavior for environments and templates created without `enable_async` must remain unchanged. Async execution should only be activated on runtimes that support async generators. Async mode must not expose `Template.module` as a synchronous module view, and callers must not receive fabricated loop length values for async iterators that do not provide length information. Support for async iterable-consuming built-in filters is limited to the filters that have async variants.
constraints.conceptual: The new async feature must be opt-in, must not regress existing synchronous template behavior, and must fail clearly where synchronous assumptions no longer hold. The library should not invent metadata such as collection length when asynchronous iteration cannot provide it reliably.

behavior: The `Environment` and `Template` constructors accept an `enable_async` option, and async execution is only active when the runtime supports async generators.
`Template.render_async()` provides coroutine-based rendering for async-enabled templates and rejects use when async mode was not enabled.

`Template.generate_async()` provides async iteration over rendered output, while `render()` and `generate()` continue to produce synchronous output by driving async execution when async mode is active.
In async mode, template calls and supported built-in filters automatically resolve awaitable results before those values participate in further rendering.
In async mode, `for` loops accept async iterables and preserve loop state such as iteration index; however, loop length is unavailable for async iterators that do not expose a length.
Includes, imports, macros, and blocks are executable in async mode, and async module creation is exposed through `Template.make_module_async()`.
`Template.module` is unavailable in async mode and must raise a runtime error instead of exposing a synchronous module interface.
acceptance_criteria: Given an `Environment(enable_async=True)` or `Template(..., enable_async=True)` on a supported Python runtime, when a template iterates over an async iterable, it should render each yielded item in order.

Given async mode is enabled, when a template expression evaluates a helper call or supported built-in filter that returns an awaitable, it should render the awaited value rather than the awaitable object.
Given async mode is enabled, when the caller uses `render_async()`, it should return the fully rendered template content through async execution.
Given async mode is enabled, when the caller uses `generate_async()`, it should expose rendered output as an async iterator.

Given async mode is enabled, when the caller uses `render()` or `generate()` instead of the async entry points, it should still produce rendered output rather than failing only because async execution is involved.
Given async mode is enabled, when code accesses `Template.module`, it should fail with a runtime error instead of returning a module object.
Given an async iterator without a known length in an async-mode loop, when template logic requires loop length, it should fail explicitly rather than returning an inferred value.

task_5.title: Add configurable environment policies for filter defaults and safe JSON output
task_5.description: Jinja2 2.9 introduces environment-level policies that control default rendering behavior. This changes how `urlize` generates link attributes, adds a built-in `tojson` filter for HTML-safe JSON serialization with configurable dumping behavior, and exposes related policy-based compatibility controls.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to Jinja2 2.9 adds environment-level policies for filter defaults and related rendering behavior, so applications can centrally control safer `urlize` output, built-in JSON serialization through `tojson`, and compatibility-sensitive string handling where supported.

expectation.grounded: Expose an `Environment.policies` mapping initialized from default policy values. The `urlize` filter must honor policy-driven defaults for `urlize.rel` and `urlize.target`, merge any explicit `rel` value with policy-defined rel tokens, and include `nofollow` in the rel set when requested. The `jinja2.utils.urlize` API must accept a `rel` value for link attributes. Add the `tojson` filter, which serializes values through the configured `json.dumps_function` and `json.dumps_kwargs`, supports an optional `indent` argument, and produces HTML-safe JSON output. Support the `compiler.ascii_str` policy for string compilation behavior on supported runtimes.
expectation.conceptual: The upgraded library should let users configure rendering defaults once at the environment level instead of hardcoding them in every template call. URL auto-linking should apply safer default link metadata and allow centralized overrides, templates should gain a built-in JSON serialization filter suitable for HTML output, and compatibility-related string behavior should remain configurable through policies.

constraints.grounded: Policy changes must affect observable defaults without breaking existing filter entry points. If `urlize.rel` is unset, generated links must omit the rel attribute unless the call supplies rel-related behavior. If a `target` argument is passed directly to `urlize`, it must take precedence over the policy default. `tojson` must continue to support custom dump functions and keyword arguments through policies while allowing per-call indentation overrides. Autoescaped template contexts must preserve the filter's safe HTML rendering contract.
constraints.conceptual: The new policy system should refine default rendering behavior without removing normal template customization. Explicit caller choices should override environment defaults, disabling a default should stop that output from appearing, and JSON output should stay safely embeddable in HTML-oriented template contexts.

behavior: New environments expose a `policies` mapping with defaults for `compiler.ascii_str`, `urlize.rel`, `urlize.target`, `json.dumps_function`, and `json.dumps_kwargs`.
Rendering `urlize` without overrides now adds a `rel` attribute derived from the environment policy, which defaults to `noopener`.
When `nofollow=True` is used with `urlize`, `nofollow` is added to the rendered rel tokens instead of being handled as a separate dedicated flag.
When a `rel` value is provided to `urlize`, it is combined with the policy-defined rel tokens and rendered as a normalized rel attribute.
When `urlize` is called without a `target`, the rendered link target is taken from the environment policy if one is configured.
The low-level `jinja2.utils.urlize` interface now uses a `rel` argument to control rendered link relationship attributes.
Templates now support a `tojson` filter that serializes values into HTML-safe JSON output and supports optional pretty-print indentation.
The `tojson` filter uses policy-configured dump behavior, including a custom dump function and default dump keyword arguments, with sorted keys enabled by default unless overridden.
String compilation behavior is now policy-controlled through `compiler.ascii_str` on runtimes where that distinction is relevant.
acceptance_criteria: When an application creates a new environment in 2.9, it should be able to inspect and modify default rendering policies through `Environment.policies` before rendering templates.
When a template uses `urlize` with no explicit rel configuration, generated links should include the environment's default rel behavior, and the out-of-the-box default should add `noopener`.
When an application disables the `urlize.rel` policy, `urlize` output should stop emitting a rel attribute unless the template call explicitly requests rel-related output.
When a template uses `urlize(nofollow=True)`, the rendered link should include `nofollow` alongside any other rel tokens that apply.
When an environment sets a default `urlize.target` and a template does not pass a target argument, generated links should use the configured default target.

When a template uses `tojson`, it should render serialized JSON that is safe for HTML-oriented template output and should honor any environment-configured dump function, dump options, and per-call indentation.

task_6.title: Harden urlize links with default noopener rel
task_6.description: The 2.9 upgrade changes Jinja's URL auto-linking so generated anchors are safer by default. `urlize` now applies a default `rel` policy of `noopener`, exposes explicit relationship control, and resolves link `rel` and `target` values through environment policies when not provided directly.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that URL auto-linking through `urlize` produces opener-safe links by default while remaining configurable for relationship and target attributes through the supported public API.

expectation.grounded: Templates using the `urlize` filter and callers using `jinja2.utils.urlize` should render anchor tags with a `rel` attribute derived from the effective relationship configuration. The `urlize` filter should accept a `rel` argument, combine it with `nofollow=True` and `Environment.policies['urlize.rel']`, remove duplicate relationship tokens, and apply `Environment.policies['urlize.target']` when no explicit target is passed. Jinja's default policy should contribute `noopener`, and direct calls to `jinja2.utils.urlize` should accept `rel` as the public way to control rendered link relationships.
expectation.conceptual: Auto-linked URLs should become safer by default by adding opener protection to generated links. Callers should still be able to control link relationship tokens and target behavior explicitly or through environment-level defaults, and `nofollow` should continue to affect the rendered relationship attribute rather than being dropped.

constraints.grounded: Existing URL, email, escaping, and trimming behavior of `urlize` should remain unchanged except for the new computation of `rel` and policy-backed `target` values. The `rel` attribute should be omitted when the effective relationship configuration is empty, explicit target values should still be honored, and combined relationship tokens should not be duplicated.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should not change what text is recognized as a link or how links are escaped and shortened, beyond adding the new relationship metadata and policy-driven target defaults. Consumers must be able to disable the default relationship metadata or override it without causing duplicate or conflicting link attributes.

behavior: By default, links generated through `urlize` include `rel="noopener"`.
The `urlize` filter accepts a `rel` argument and merges it with the environment's default relationship policy into one rendered `rel` attribute.
When `nofollow=True` is supplied to the `urlize` filter, the rendered `rel` attribute includes `nofollow` alongside any other effective relationship tokens.
When the effective relationship token set is empty, `urlize` renders no `rel` attribute.
When no `target` argument is passed to the `urlize` filter, it uses the environment's default target policy; when a target is provided, that target is rendered on the generated anchor.
Direct calls to `jinja2.utils.urlize` use a `rel` parameter to control rendered link relationship tokens.
acceptance_criteria: When plain text containing a URL is rendered through `urlize` with default settings, the generated anchor should include opener protection in its `rel` attribute.
When a caller provides `rel` values and the environment also defines default relationship values, the generated anchor should contain the union of those relationship tokens without duplicates.
When `nofollow=True` is used with `urlize`, the generated anchor should include `nofollow` in the rendered `rel` attribute.
When relationship defaults are cleared and no explicit relationship tokens are provided, `urlize` should render links without a `rel` attribute.

When a default target is configured and no explicit target is passed to `urlize`, the generated anchor should use the configured target; when an explicit target is passed, that explicit target should be used instead.
When `jinja2.utils.urlize` is called directly with a `rel` value, the generated anchor should render that relationship metadata.

task_7.title: Support attribute fallback for legacy Python 2 classes
task_7.description: The 2.9 update restores item-to-attribute fallback during lookup resolution for legacy Python 2 old-style class instances. When item-style access fails with an attribute-related error, Jinja should continue trying attribute access so existing template lookups can still resolve the expected value.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that item-preferred lookups still fall back to object attributes for old-style Python 2 class instances when item access fails with an attribute-related error, so existing templates and callers can resolve available attributes instead of failing the lookup early.

expectation.grounded: In `Environment.getitem`, a failed `obj[argument]` lookup that raises `AttributeError` must enter the same fallback path as `TypeError` and `LookupError`. When `argument` is a string and the target object exposes a matching attribute, the attribute value should be returned. If no matching attribute exists, the method should preserve its existing undefined-result behavior.
expectation.conceptual: Lookups that normally try subscript access first should remain compatible with legacy Python 2 objects whose failed item access surfaces as an attribute error. If the requested name exists as an attribute, users should see that value resolved instead of an unexpected failed lookup.

constraints.grounded: Preserve the existing item-first lookup order in `Environment.getitem`. Successful item access must continue to take precedence over attributes, and missing values must continue to follow the library's existing undefined handling after both lookup paths are exhausted.
constraints.conceptual: Do not change normal lookup precedence or general mapping behavior. The update should only broaden fallback compatibility for affected legacy objects without altering successful existing resolutions.

behavior: `Environment.getitem` now treats `AttributeError` raised during item access as a recoverable lookup failure that can trigger attribute fallback.
For string lookup names, if item access fails and the target object has a same-named attribute, the attribute value is returned.
If item access succeeds, its result still wins over attribute fallback.
If neither item access nor attribute access resolves the requested name, the existing undefined outcome remains unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When a caller or template performs an item-preferred lookup for a string name on a Python 2 old-style class instance whose item access raises `AttributeError` and whose attribute exists, it should resolve to that attribute value.
When the same lookup can be satisfied through item access, it should continue returning the item value rather than switching to the attribute value.
When item access fails and no corresponding attribute is available, the lookup should continue producing the library's normal undefined result instead of introducing a new hard failure.

task_9.title: Restore Cycler.next compatibility on Python 3
task_9.description: Version 2.9 restores the public `Cycler.next()` behavior for Python 3 users while preserving normal iterator behavior. This update fixes compatibility for code and templates that expect `Cycler` to expose a callable `next` method and keeps cycling state progression consistent.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.9 restores Python 3 compatibility for `Cycler` by making the helper expose a callable `next()` method again, without changing its existing cycling semantics.

expectation.grounded: `jinja2.utils.Cycler` must provide a public `next()` method on Python 3. Calling `Cycler.next()` must return the current item and then advance the internal position to the next item in the cycle. Iterator-style access through `__next__` must continue to behave the same as `next()`.
expectation.conceptual: Users should be able to advance a `Cycler` with either its explicit `next()` method or normal iterator usage, and both forms should produce the same sequence and state transitions.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve existing `Cycler` semantics for `current`, wraparound cycling, and reset behavior. Restoring `next()` must not remove or change `__next__` behavior for Python 3 iterator consumers.
constraints.conceptual: The compatibility fix should add back the missing public method without altering how cycling, rewinding, or iterator consumption already works.

behavior: `Cycler` exposes `next()` again for Python 3 callers.
Each call to `Cycler.next()` returns the same item that is currently exposed via `Cycler.current` before advancing.
After `Cycler.next()` is called, the current position advances by one item and wraps to the beginning after the last item.
`Cycler.__next__` remains available and is behaviorally equivalent to `Cycler.next()`.
acceptance_criteria: When a `Cycler` is created with multiple items on Python 3, calling `next()` on the object should succeed and return the current item instead of failing due to a missing method.
When `next()` is called repeatedly on a `Cycler`, it should yield items in cycle order and continue again from the first item after the last item.
When `current` is inspected before and after a `next()` call, it should reflect that `next()` returns the pre-advance item and then moves the cycle forward.
When the built-in iterator protocol is used on `Cycler`, it should remain consistent with the explicit `next()` method.
When `reset()` is called after one or more advances, the cycle should return to its initial position.

task_8.title: Support top-level set statements in extended templates
task_8.description: The upgrade adds support for using top-level Jinja set statements, including block capture form, in templates that extend a parent template. Assigned values are preserved in the rendered template context and exported consistently, and captured block values follow the active autoescape behavior without being treated as direct output.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates using `{% extends %}` can define top-level variables with `{% set %}` statements, including block capture form, and have those assignments available during rendering just like other top-level template state.

expectation.grounded: In templates that use `{% extends %}`, top-level `Assign` and `AssignBlock` statements must be compiled as valid assignments rather than rejected as output-producing content. Assigned names should be recorded in `context.vars` at top level, and non-private names should be added to `context.exported_vars`. For block-style `set`, the captured value should be materialized according to the current autoescape evaluation context so the assigned result preserves normal escaped-versus-markup behavior.
expectation.conceptual: A child template should be able to define top-level variables, including captured block values, before or alongside inheritance logic. Those variables should behave like normal top-level template assignments: available where rendering needs them, exported when public, and handled with the same escaping semantics users see elsewhere.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve existing top-level export rules: assigned names remain stored for template context lookup, but names starting with `_` are not exported as public variables. Block `set` in an extended template must remain non-output-producing while still making its captured value available as an assignment. Normal top-level assignment tracking must continue to work for one or multiple assigned names.
constraints.conceptual: Inheritance support for top-level assignments must not leak private variables, must not turn captured assignments into rendered output, and must keep assignment visibility consistent whether one or many variables are defined.

behavior: A template that extends another template may execute a top-level `{% set name = ... %}` assignment and have the assigned value retained in the template context.
A template that extends another template may execute a top-level block capture `{% set name %}...{% endset %}` assignment without that block being treated as forbidden rendered output.
Top-level assigned variables are propagated into the template context storage used during rendering, including when multiple names are assigned across top-level set statements.
Top-level assigned names that do not begin with `_` are exposed as exported template variables, while underscore-prefixed names remain non-public.
Values captured by block-style `set` respect the current autoescape mode so the resulting assigned value has the same observable escaping behavior as other rendered template content.
acceptance_criteria: When a child template uses `{% extends %}` and defines a top-level `{% set x = value %}`, rendering should succeed and `x` should be available to inherited rendering logic that reads it.

When a child template uses `{% extends %}` and defines a top-level `{% set x %}...{% endset %}`, rendering should succeed without treating the captured block as direct output, and the assigned value should be available where `x` is referenced.
When multiple top-level variables are assigned in an extended template, each assigned name should be present in the runtime template context after assignment.
When a top-level assigned name is public, it should be exported as a template variable; when its name starts with `_`, it should remain non-exported.
When block-style `set` runs under autoescaping, the assigned value should preserve the expected escaped-versus-safe behavior for that evaluation context.

task_10.title: Align undefined subtraction with standard undefined operator behavior
task_10.description: The upgrade makes subtraction with undefined template values behave consistently with other arithmetic and access operations. Instead of falling through to Python's default subtraction handling, undefined operands now use Jinja's normal undefined failure behavior so template authors get the expected undefined-value error semantics.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that subtraction expressions involving undefined template values behave consistently with other operations on undefined values and report the framework's standard undefined-value failure instead of inconsistent operator behavior.

expectation.grounded: Jinja's `Undefined` behavior must treat subtraction the same way as its other unsupported arithmetic operations. Both forward subtraction (`undefined - value`) and reverse subtraction (`value - undefined`) should route through `Undefined`'s normal failure path and raise `UndefinedError` when evaluated.
expectation.conceptual: When a template performs subtraction and either side is undefined, the operation should fail in the same predictable way as other invalid uses of undefined values, using the template engine's undefined-value error semantics.

constraints.grounded: This change is limited to subtraction behavior for `Undefined` values and must preserve the existing behavior of other operators and comparisons. Equality, truthiness, rendering of plain undefined output, and already-failing undefined operations should remain unchanged.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should only remove the inconsistency around subtraction on undefined values and should not alter unrelated undefined-value behaviors that users already rely on.

behavior: Evaluating a subtraction where the left operand is an undefined value now raises `UndefinedError` instead of relying on Python's default subtraction fallback.
Evaluating a subtraction where the right operand is an undefined value now raises `UndefinedError` through the same undefined-value handling path.
Subtraction on undefined values is now consistent with the way other invalid arithmetic-style operations on undefined values already fail.
acceptance_criteria: When a template evaluates an expression equivalent to `undefined - value`, it should raise `UndefinedError`.
When a template evaluates an expression equivalent to `value - undefined`, it should raise `UndefinedError`.
When undefined values are used in non-subtraction scenarios that already had established behavior, those outcomes should remain unchanged after the upgrade.
When users encounter subtraction with undefined values, the failure mode should match the framework's standard undefined-value behavior rather than a generic Python operator error.

task_11.title: Improve errors for unquoted callable names in sequence filters
task_11.description: Jinja2 2.9 improves runtime diagnostics when sequence filters dispatch to a filter or test by name and that name was passed as an unquoted template variable. Instead of only reporting a missing filter or test, the runtime now exposes the undefined-name context and adds a clearer hint that the callable name may need to be quoted.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that `map` and related sequence-selection filters report actionable runtime errors when a filter or test name is passed without quotes, so template authors can distinguish a missing callable from an accidentally undefined template variable.

expectation.grounded: When `Environment.call_filter` or `Environment.call_test` cannot resolve a callable name and the provided name is an `Undefined` value, they should raise `TemplateRuntimeError` with the missing-filter or missing-test failure and an additional hint that the callable name may need quoting. This should be observable through template features that delegate by callable name, including `map`, `select`, `reject`, `selectattr`, and `rejectattr`.
expectation.conceptual: If a template uses a filter or test name dynamically in a sequence helper but forgets to quote it, rendering should fail with a clearer error that points to the unquoted-name mistake rather than only saying the callable was missing.

constraints.grounded: Do not change successful execution for valid filter or test names. Preserve existing behavior for `map(attribute=...)`, existing argument validation when `map` is missing its filter argument or receives unexpected keywords, and the existing boolean fallback behavior of `select`, `reject`, `selectattr`, and `rejectattr` when no test is provided.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should only improve error reporting for the unquoted-callable case. Normal filter and test execution, attribute-based mapping, and default truthiness-based selection behavior should continue to work as before.

behavior: Calling a filter by name through `map` should surface a clearer `TemplateRuntimeError` when the callable name is undefined because it was not quoted in the template.

Calling a test by name through `select`, `reject`, `selectattr`, or `rejectattr` should surface the same kind of clearer `TemplateRuntimeError` when the test name is undefined because it was not quoted.
The missing-callable error should retain whether the failed lookup was for a filter or a test, while also exposing that the supplied name came from an undefined value.
Sequence helpers should continue to behave the same for valid quoted callable names and for modes that do not depend on callable-name lookup.
acceptance_criteria: When `map` is given an unquoted filter name that resolves to an undefined template value, rendering should raise `TemplateRuntimeError` that identifies a missing filter and includes guidance that the name may need to be quoted.

When `select`, `reject`, `selectattr`, or `rejectattr` is given an unquoted test name that resolves to an undefined template value, rendering should raise `TemplateRuntimeError` that identifies a missing test and includes guidance that the name may need to be quoted.
When a valid quoted filter or test name is provided to these helpers, behavior and output should remain unchanged.
When `map` is used in attribute mode or when select-style helpers are used without an explicit test, the existing non-error behavior should remain unchanged.

task_13.title: Update truncate filter tolerance behavior
task_13.description: Version 2.9 changes the `truncate` filter so strings that only exceed the requested length by a small tolerance are no longer truncated by default, and it exposes that tolerance as a configurable public parameter.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.9 preserves and documents the new `truncate` filter behavior so content that only barely exceeds the configured length is left intact by default, while callers can still force truncation when needed.

expectation.grounded: The `truncate` filter must accept a fourth public argument, `leeway`, with a default of `5`. A string should be returned unchanged when its length is less than or equal to `length + leeway`. When truncation is required, `killwords=True` should cut strictly at `length - len(end)` and append `end`, while the default word-preserving mode should truncate at the last space before that cutoff and append `end` without inserting an extra separator. Invalid argument combinations where `length` is shorter than `end` or `leeway` is negative must be rejected.
expectation.conceptual: The truncation API should treat near-boundary values more leniently by default: text that only slightly exceeds the target length should remain unmodified, but callers must be able to opt into stricter truncation and still choose whether truncation preserves whole words or cuts mid-word.

constraints.grounded: Existing `truncate` parameters for target length, `killwords`, and custom `end` markers must remain supported. The observable return value must stay unchanged for inputs already within the tolerated limit, and truncation must still include the configured `end` marker within the requested limit calculation. The filter must not silently accept negative `leeway` values or an `end` marker longer than the requested length.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade must remain backward-compatible for normal `truncate` usage while adding stricter validation around nonsensical argument values. Any custom suffix should continue to count toward the visible truncation limit, and the new tolerance should not alter strings that already fit comfortably within the configured threshold.

behavior: The `truncate` filter now exposes a configurable tolerance parameter named `leeway`.
By default, strings whose length exceeds the requested limit by at most 5 characters are no longer truncated.
Callers can force the pre-2.9 strict behavior by setting `leeway` to 0.
In word-preserving mode, truncation removes the trailing partial word before appending the configured ending marker, without adding an extra space before that marker.
In `killwords` mode, truncation still slices at the character boundary needed to keep the configured ending marker within the requested length.
The filter now rejects invalid configurations where the requested length is shorter than the ending marker or the tolerance is negative.
acceptance_criteria: When `truncate` is called with default settings and the input length exceeds `length` by 5 characters or fewer, it should return the original string unchanged.
When `truncate` is called with `leeway=0` and the input exceeds `length`, it should truncate according to the configured word-preserving or word-cutting mode.
When `truncate` runs in the default word-preserving mode, it should append the configured ending marker directly after the retained content without inserting an additional space.
When `truncate` runs with `killwords=True`, it should return content cut to fit the configured ending marker within the requested total length.
When `truncate` is called with a negative `leeway`, it should fail instead of producing a truncated string.
When `truncate` is called with an ending marker longer than `length`, it should fail instead of producing output.

task_12.title: Require MarkupSafe 0.23+ for sandboxed format handling
task_12.description: Version 2.9 raises the minimum supported MarkupSafe version to 0.23 and relies on that formatter support so sandboxed template formatting remains available and continues to enforce sandbox access and escaping behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that upgrading to 2.9 requires MarkupSafe 0.23 or later and that sandboxed template formatting through `format` continues to work safely and consistently for plain text and markup-aware values.

expectation.grounded: The package must declare `MarkupSafe>=0.23` as a required dependency. In `SandboxedEnvironment`, bound `format` calls on text and `Markup` values should be recognized and processed through the sandbox formatting path, with replacement-field traversal using sandbox-controlled attribute and item access and markup-aware escaping preserved.
expectation.conceptual: After the upgrade, installations should fail fast on unsupported MarkupSafe versions, and applications using sandboxed templates should be able to rely on `format`-based interpolation remaining available without bypassing sandbox protections or markup escaping behavior.

constraints.grounded: Do not weaken sandbox enforcement: attribute lookups triggered by `format` fields must still go through sandbox attribute access rules, item lookups must still go through sandbox item access rules, and unrelated callable handling should remain unchanged. Compatibility with MarkupSafe releases below 0.23 must not be assumed.
constraints.conceptual: The dependency floor can increase, but the upgrade must not relax security boundaries or change unrelated template behavior.

behavior: Installing or resolving version 2.9 now requires `MarkupSafe` version 0.23 or higher.
Sandboxed template execution treats bound `format` methods as supported formatter entry points instead of gating them behind optional runtime feature detection.
When sandboxed `format` field resolution traverses attributes, it uses sandbox-controlled attribute access semantics.
When sandboxed `format` field resolution traverses indexes or keys, it uses sandbox-controlled item access semantics.
Formatting of markup-aware values in sandboxed templates continues through the escape-aware formatter path so escaping semantics remain active.
acceptance_criteria: When version 2.9 is installed with dependency resolution enabled, it should require `MarkupSafe>=0.23`.
When a sandboxed template invokes `format` on a text value, it should be handled as a supported formatting operation rather than being ignored as unavailable.
When a sandboxed `format` expression accesses attributes or items inside replacement fields, it should honor the same sandbox restrictions as other template attribute and item access.
When a sandboxed template formats a `Markup` value, it should preserve markup-aware escaping behavior during formatting.

task_16.title: Mark block set assignments safe under autoescape
task_16.description: The update changes block-form set assignments so captured template content is treated as safe markup when autoescaping is enabled. This prevents captured fragments from being escaped a second time when reused, while still escaping unsafe values inside the block during capture and allowing top-level block assignments to behave consistently.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that content captured with block-form `set` is treated as safe by default in autoescaped templates so reusable template fragments are not double-escaped, while unsafe values rendered inside the block remain escaped appropriately and top-level block assignments continue to work consistently.

expectation.grounded: In Jinja2 2.9, a block-form `set` assignment (`{% set name %}...{% endset %}`) should capture the rendered block body and, when autoescaping is active, expose the assigned value as safe `Markup` rather than an ordinary escaped string. Rendering that assigned variable later should preserve intended markup without escaping the whole captured fragment again, while interpolated values inside the block are still escaped according to the active autoescape policy before capture. Block-form `set` should also be allowed at template top level in situations where normal output checks would otherwise interfere, such as inherited templates.
expectation.conceptual: Captured template fragments assigned with block-style `set` should behave like already-safe rendered content in autoescaped environments. Users should see untrusted values sanitized inside the captured fragment, but should not see the entire fragment escaped again when the variable is rendered later. The same construct should work reliably even when used at the top level of a template.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the observable behavior of ordinary expression-based `set` assignments. When autoescaping is disabled, block-form `set` should continue to behave like normal captured output without introducing extra escaping behavior. Unsafe values rendered inside a block-form `set` must still be escaped during capture under autoescaping, and top-level assigned names should remain available/exported according to existing template semantics.
constraints.conceptual: Only the safety status of captured block assignments should change in autoescaped rendering. Existing assignment behavior outside that case should remain stable, and the update must not weaken escaping of untrusted content inserted into the captured block.

behavior: A block-form `set` assignment now captures rendered block output as safe content when autoescaping is enabled.
Rendering a variable produced by block-form `set` should no longer escape the captured markup a second time.
Values interpolated inside the block-form `set` body are still escaped according to the active autoescape rules before the final captured value is stored.
Block-form `set` can be used at template top level without being blocked by output-check restrictions, including in templates that participate in inheritance.
acceptance_criteria: When autoescaping is enabled and a template captures markup with block-form `set`, rendering the assigned variable later should preserve that markup instead of escaping the full fragment again.
When untrusted input is interpolated inside a block-form `set` in an autoescaped template, the interpolated value should be escaped within the captured fragment.
When autoescaping is disabled, block-form `set` should continue to behave like normal captured output without new safe-marking side effects visible to template users.

When a template uses block-form `set` at top level, including in an inherited template flow, the assignment should succeed and the assigned variable should remain usable like other top-level set values.

task_15.title: Add configurable HTML-safe JSON rendering with `tojson`
task_15.description: Jinja 2.9 introduces a built-in `tojson` template filter and a new `Environment.policies` configuration surface so applications can render values as HTML-safe JSON in templates and customize the JSON serializer and its default options.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates can serialize values through a built-in `tojson` filter, and allow applications to configure how that JSON is produced through environment-level policies while keeping the rendered output safe for HTML embedding.

expectation.grounded: `Environment` should expose a `policies` mapping initialized from default policy values. Templates should provide a `tojson` filter that serializes values using `Environment.policies['json.dumps_function']` when configured, otherwise the default JSON dumper, and `Environment.policies['json.dumps_kwargs']` as the default serializer options. The filter should accept an optional `indent` argument for pretty-printing and should produce HTML-safe JSON by escaping `<`, `>`, `&`, and apostrophes in string content.
expectation.conceptual: Applications should be able to render JSON directly from templates with `|tojson`, optionally pretty-printed, and centrally control the serializer and its default options through environment configuration. The rendered JSON should be safe to embed in HTML and script contexts.

constraints.grounded: JSON serialization settings should be environment-scoped defaults rather than per-template hardcoding. Supplying `indent` to `tojson` should augment the serializer options for that render without requiring a global policy change. The HTML-safety guarantees are intended for HTML contexts and do not remove the need for additional escaping or different quoting when the result is inserted into double-quoted HTML attributes.
constraints.conceptual: Configuration should remain centralized and reusable across templates, while one-off pretty-printing remains possible at the usage site. The feature should improve safe HTML embedding without changing the need for context-appropriate escaping in placements that remain unsafe, such as double-quoted attributes.

behavior: A new `tojson` template filter is available in the standard filter set.
`tojson` serializes the input value to JSON using the environment's configured JSON dumper and serializer keyword arguments.
If `Environment.policies['json.dumps_function']` is not configured, the default JSON serialization function is used.
If `Environment.policies['json.dumps_kwargs']` is configured, those options are applied to JSON serialization by default; the built-in defaults include sorted object keys.
Passing `indent` to `tojson` enables pretty-printed output for that rendering operation.
The JSON output escapes `<`, `>`, `&`, and apostrophes inside strings so the result is safe for HTML and `<script>` embedding, with the documented exception of double-quoted HTML attributes.
acceptance_criteria: When a template applies `|tojson` to a value, it should render that value as JSON without requiring a custom filter.
When no custom JSON policy is configured, `|tojson` should use the library's default JSON serialization behavior and default dump options.
When an application sets `Environment.policies['json.dumps_function']`, `|tojson` should use that serializer for output generation.
When an application sets `Environment.policies['json.dumps_kwargs']`, `|tojson` should apply those values as the default serializer configuration.
When `|tojson(indent=...)` is used, the rendered JSON should be pretty-printed according to the requested indentation level.
When serialized strings contain `<`, `>`, `&`, or apostrophes, the rendered JSON should escape those characters so it can be embedded safely in HTML or script content.
When `|tojson` output is placed in a double-quoted HTML attribute, applications should still treat that placement as requiring additional escaping or a different quoting strategy.

task_14.title: Use call-time autoescape for macros
task_14.description: Jinja 2.9 changes macro rendering so escaping is determined when a macro is invoked instead of when it is defined. This aligns macro output with the caller's active autoescape mode, preserves compatibility for direct macro calls without an explicit evaluation context, and resolves omitted macro defaults during execution rather than prebinding them at definition time.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that macros honor the active autoescaping mode at the point they are invoked, and that omitted macro parameters are resolved during macro execution so returned output and defaulted values reflect the caller's current rendering context.

expectation.grounded: Compiled macros exposed through `jinja2.runtime.Macro` should determine whether to return a `Markup` result or plain text from the invocation's `EvalContext.autoescape` value. If `Macro.__call__` is invoked without an `EvalContext`, it should fall back to the macro's default autoescape setting. Macro parameters that are not provided by the caller should remain missing until macro execution, so any declared default expressions are applied inside the macro body rather than being pre-evaluated when the macro is defined.
expectation.conceptual: A macro should be escaped based on where it is used, not where it was declared. When callers omit macro arguments, defaults should be applied when the macro runs so the macro sees the current rendering context for those values.

constraints.grounded: Calling a `Macro` object without an explicit `EvalContext` must remain supported. Existing macro argument validation for unsupported keyword arguments and too many positional arguments should remain unchanged. The change should only alter escaping and missing-argument resolution semantics, not the macro call surface.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should preserve existing macro calling compatibility and validation rules while changing only when escaping and default values are decided.

behavior: A macro invoked in an autoescaped rendering context should produce a safe escaped result even if the macro was defined while autoescaping was disabled.
A macro invoked in a non-autoescaped rendering context should produce plain text even if the macro was defined while autoescaping was enabled.

When `jinja2.runtime.Macro.__call__` receives an `EvalContext` as its first argument, it should use that `EvalContext.autoescape` value to decide whether to wrap the return value as `Markup`; when no eval context is supplied, it should use the macro's default autoescape behavior.

If a macro parameter is omitted, the call should pass it through as missing and let the macro body resolve any declared default during that invocation; excess positional arguments and unexpected keyword arguments should continue to raise `TypeError`.
acceptance_criteria: Given a macro defined with autoescaping disabled, when it is called from an autoescaped context and returns text containing HTML markup, then the rendered result should follow the caller's autoescaped behavior rather than the definition-time behavior.

Given a macro defined with autoescaping enabled, when it is called from a non-autoescaped context, then the rendered result should remain unescaped rather than inheriting the definition-time escaping decision.
When a caller invokes a `jinja2.runtime.Macro` object without passing an `EvalContext`, it should still render successfully using its default autoescape behavior.
When a macro argument is omitted and the parameter has a default expression, the default should be applied during that invocation instead of being frozen when the macro was defined.
When a caller supplies too many positional arguments or unsupported keyword arguments to a macro, the call should continue to fail with `TypeError`.

task_17.title: Make Python 2 ASCII literal coercion configurable
task_17.description: Version 2.9 adds a compiler policy that lets Python 2 applications disable automatic coercion of ASCII-only template string literals to native byte strings. The default remains compatibility-oriented, but users can now preserve unicode/text values for ASCII literals when needed.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that on Python 2, applications can disable automatic ASCII-byte coercion for ASCII-only template string literals through the compiler policy system, while preserving the previous compatibility behavior by default and leaving non-ASCII text unaffected.

expectation.grounded: Expose a `compiler.ascii_str` entry on `Environment.policies` with a default enabled state. On Python 2, this policy must control whether ASCII-only template string constants are surfaced as native `str` values or preserved as unicode/text values. When the policy is disabled, ASCII-only string literals and constant-folded string expressions must remain unicode/text. When enabled, ASCII-only unicode/text constants may be converted to native `str`, but values that cannot be represented as ASCII must remain unicode/text.
expectation.conceptual: Upgrading to 2.9 should let Python 2 users opt out of legacy ASCII coercion for template literals. With the default setting, existing templates should keep their prior byte-string-compatible behavior for ASCII-only literals. When the option is turned off, those literals should stay as text/unicode, and literals containing non-ASCII characters should continue to stay as text regardless of the setting.

constraints.grounded: This policy change applies only to Python 2 handling of template string constants. It must not change Python 3 behavior, must not force non-ASCII text through ASCII conversion, and must not alter the handling of non-string constants or unrelated environment policies.
constraints.conceptual: The new option should narrowly affect legacy Python 2 string typing behavior for ASCII-only template literals. It should not create regressions in other runtimes, other data types, or text that contains non-ASCII characters.

behavior: A new `compiler.ascii_str` environment policy is available and defaults to the legacy compatibility behavior.
On Python 2 with `compiler.ascii_str` enabled, ASCII-only template string literals can be exposed as native byte strings (`str`).
On Python 2 with `compiler.ascii_str` disabled, ASCII-only template string literals are preserved as unicode/text values.
Template string literals containing non-ASCII characters remain unicode/text on Python 2 regardless of the `compiler.ascii_str` setting.
The policy applies to compiled constant string values, including constant expressions processed during compilation or optimization.
acceptance_criteria: When a Python 2 environment uses the default policy settings, rendering or evaluating a template expression that contains an ASCII-only string literal should continue to expose that literal as native `str`.

When a Python 2 environment sets `Environment.policies['compiler.ascii_str']` to `False`, an ASCII-only string literal used in a template expression should be preserved as unicode/text when observed through filters or other template operations.
When a Python 2 template literal contains non-ASCII characters, it should remain unicode/text whether `compiler.ascii_str` is enabled or disabled.
When the application is running on Python 3, this policy should not introduce a behavioral change in template string handling.
When a string value is produced from a constant template expression rather than a raw token alone, the same `compiler.ascii_str` behavior should still be observed.

task_18.title: Refine `is` test argument parsing for boolean test expressions
task_18.description: Template `is` tests now treat the first test argument as a restricted primary expression instead of an unrestricted expression. This removes ambiguous parsing around boolean operators so multiple test expressions can be combined naturally, but it also narrows what syntax is accepted as the immediate first argument to a test.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that template `is` test expressions can be combined with boolean operators such as `and` and `or` without requiring extra parentheses, while restricting the first argument passed to a test so it is not interpreted as an arbitrary expression.

expectation.grounded: When parsing template expressions that use `is`, the first positional argument supplied to a test must be treated as a primary expression rather than a full expression. As a result, boolean operators following that first argument must separate outer expressions, allowing multiple `is` tests to be written in a single boolean expression without extra grouping.
expectation.conceptual: Template authors should be able to write multiple `is` checks in one boolean expression and have each check evaluated independently. A test's first argument should behave like a single direct value, not like an unrestricted inline expression that can absorb later boolean logic.

constraints.grounded: Do not allow the immediate first argument to an `is` test to consume arbitrary compound expressions or trailing boolean operators. Preserve normal behavior for existing `is` tests whose first argument is already a simple primary value.
constraints.conceptual: Fix the parsing ambiguity without changing unrelated expression behavior. Existing straightforward test usage should keep working, but overly broad first-argument syntax should no longer be accepted.

behavior: The first positional operand after an `is` test name is parsed as a primary expression instead of a full expression.
Boolean operators that appear after that operand terminate the current test argument and join separate outer expressions.
Multiple `is` test expressions can be written in one boolean expression without requiring extra parentheses solely to avoid parser ambiguity.
Arbitrary compound expressions are no longer accepted as the immediate first argument to an `is` test.
acceptance_criteria: When a template expression combines one `is` test with another using `and` or `or`, it should parse and evaluate as two separate test expressions without needing extra parentheses for disambiguation.
When a boolean operator appears after the first argument to an `is` test, it should act as boolean logic between expressions rather than being consumed as part of that test argument.
When a template uses an `is` test with a simple primary first argument, it should continue to parse and behave as before.
When a template provides an arbitrary compound expression as the immediate first argument to an `is` test, that syntax should no longer be accepted as a valid unrestricted test argument.

task_20.title: Make with and autoescape tags built in
task_20.description: Version 2.9 promotes the template `with` and `autoescape` tags from opt-in extensions to built-in language features, so templates can use them without explicit extension registration while preserving their scoped assignment and scoped autoescaping behavior.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that templates can use the `with` and `autoescape` block tags by default in 2.9, without requiring opt-in extension setup, while preserving the same scoped variable-binding and scoped autoescaping behavior users expect from those tags.

expectation.grounded: The template parser must recognize `with` and `autoescape` as built-in statement keywords. Environments should no longer require `jinja2.ext.WithExtension` or `jinja2.ext.AutoEscapeExtension` for these tags to parse and execute. A `with` block must still accept one or more assignment expressions and apply those bindings only within the block body until `endwith`. An `autoescape` block must still accept an autoescape expression, apply that setting only within the block body until `endautoescape`, and restore outer behavior after the block.
expectation.conceptual: Users upgrading to 2.9 should be able to write `with` and `autoescape` blocks in templates out of the box. Those blocks should behave the same as before from a template author’s perspective: `with` provides temporary scoped variables, and `autoescape` temporarily changes escaping rules only for the enclosed content.

constraints.grounded: Built-in support must remain compatible with the existing public tag syntax and closing tags for `with`/`endwith` and `autoescape`/`endautoescape`. The change must not require extension-specific registration for successful parsing of these tags, and block-local effects must not leak outside their scope.
constraints.conceptual: The upgrade should remove configuration overhead without changing how template authors use these tags or weakening their scope boundaries. Temporary assignments and temporary escaping settings must stay local to the block that declared them.

behavior: Templates can use the `with` block tag without explicitly enabling a separate extension.
Templates can use the `autoescape` block tag without explicitly enabling a separate extension.
A `with` block evaluates its assignment expressions at block entry and exposes the assigned names only within that block's scope.
A `with` block supports multiple assignments in a single tag before the block body.
An `autoescape` block evaluates an autoescape expression for the block and applies that escaping policy only to the enclosed scope.
After `endwith` or `endautoescape`, the outer template scope and escaping behavior continue unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When a template uses a `with` block in an environment that does not explicitly register `jinja2.ext.WithExtension`, it should parse and render successfully.
When a template uses an `autoescape` block in an environment that does not explicitly register `jinja2.ext.AutoEscapeExtension`, it should parse and render successfully.
When a `with` block assigns one or more names, those names should be available inside the block body and should not remain newly bound outside the block after `endwith`.
When an `autoescape` block changes escaping behavior, rendering inside the block should follow that setting and rendering after `endautoescape` should revert to the enclosing behavior.
When users upgrade from 2.8.1 to 2.9, existing template syntax for `with` and `autoescape` blocks should remain valid while no longer depending on opt-in extension configuration.

task_21.title: Add built-in autoescape selection helper
task_21.description: Jinja2 2.9 adds a built-in `select_autoescape` helper so applications can configure template autoescaping from filename patterns without writing a custom callback. The helper is available from the top-level package and applies consistent defaults for common HTML and XML template types, string-based templates, and unmatched extensions.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that applications upgrading to Jinja2 2.9 can use a built-in helper to configure `Environment` autoescaping based on template name and extension, with safe defaults for common markup templates and predictable fallback behavior for string templates and unmatched filenames.

expectation.grounded: Expose a public `select_autoescape` function from `jinja2` that returns an autoescape selector callable suitable for `Environment(autoescape=...)`. The selector must enable autoescaping for template names ending in configured `enabled_extensions` values, disable it for names ending in configured `disabled_extensions` values, return `default_for_string` when the template name is `None`, and return `default` when no extension rule matches. Matching must be case-insensitive, and extension values must be accepted whether or not they include a leading dot. The default enabled extensions are `html`, `htm`, and `xml`; the default string-template behavior is enabled; the default unmatched fallback is disabled.
expectation.conceptual: The library should provide a first-class way to turn autoescaping on or off from template naming conventions instead of requiring every application to implement its own callback. Using the helper should produce consistent, case-insensitive decisions for common markup templates, sensible behavior for templates created from strings, and an explicit fallback for filenames that do not match configured rules.

constraints.grounded: The selector must make its decision only from the provided template name and the helper configuration. It must preserve explicit disable rules, preserve the caller-configured fallback values, and avoid case-sensitive mismatches for template extensions. Unmatched filenames must not be treated as enabled unless `default` is set accordingly.
constraints.conceptual: The new helper should be predictable and safe: common web template types should autoescape by default, opt-out extensions should remain opt-out, and anything not explicitly matched should follow the caller's chosen fallback instead of changing behavior implicitly.

behavior: A new public `jinja2.select_autoescape` helper is available for configuring `Environment` autoescaping.
Calling `select_autoescape(...)` returns a callable that decides the initial autoescape state from the template name.
By default, templates whose names end in `.html`, `.htm`, or `.xml` are treated as autoescaped.
If a template name ends with an extension listed in `disabled_extensions`, autoescaping is disabled for that template.
If the template name is `None`, the selector returns the configured `default_for_string` value.
If no enabled or disabled extension matches, the selector returns the configured `default` value.
Extension matching is case-insensitive.
Configured extensions are normalized so callers can pass them with or without a leading dot.
acceptance_criteria: When importing `select_autoescape` from `jinja2`, the import should succeed and the returned value should be usable as the `autoescape` argument to `Environment`.
When `select_autoescape()` is used with its defaults and a template name ends in `.html`, `.htm`, or `.xml` in any letter case, the selector should enable autoescaping.
When `disabled_extensions` contains an extension that matches the template name suffix, the selector should disable autoescaping for that template.
When the selector receives `None` as the template name, it should return the configured `default_for_string` behavior.
When a template name does not match any enabled or disabled extension, it should follow the configured `default` behavior.
When extensions are configured with or without leading dots, matching should behave the same way.

task_19.title: Normalize Context Propagation for Includes and Imports
task_19.description: Jinja2 2.9 normalizes template scoping so include and import constructs propagate caller context consistently when context sharing is enabled. This removes prior inconsistencies where included templates or imported macros could miss values from the active scope, while preserving explicit context isolation and the documented default context behavior of each construct.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that template inclusion and import operations propagate context consistently so included templates and imported macros or modules observe the same active caller data whenever context sharing is enabled, while explicit context isolation continues to work predictably.

expectation.grounded: In Jinja2 2.9, `{% include %}`, `{% include ... with context %}`, `{% import %}`, and `{% from ... import ... %}` must follow one context propagation model: when context sharing applies, the target template or imported module is evaluated against the full active `Context`, including values currently visible to the caller and values introduced in the current scope; when `without context` applies, it must use its isolated default module or rendering context instead. The remaining difference between these constructs is only their default `with context` versus `without context` behavior.
expectation.conceptual: Included templates and imported macros should either see the caller's live template data consistently or stay isolated from it, depending only on the explicit context modifier or the construct's documented default.

constraints.grounded: Do not change the documented defaults for context sharing: `include` remains context-sharing by default, while `import` and `from ... import ...` remain context-isolated by default unless `with context` is specified. `without context` must continue to prevent caller-local runtime values from affecting the included or imported template.
constraints.conceptual: Keep existing template syntax and default behavior intact, but remove inconsistent scope visibility between the different include and import forms. Explicit isolation must still isolate.

behavior: Rendering an `include` with context sharing enabled resolves variables from the complete active caller context, not just outer parent data.

Importing a template with `{% import ... with context %}` or `{% from ... import ... with context %}` binds exported macros and imported names to the same full caller context model used by context-sharing includes.
Values introduced in the current template scope become observable to included templates and context-sharing imports when they would otherwise be visible at that call site.
Using `without context` on `include`, `import`, or `from ... import ...` keeps the target template isolated from caller-local runtime values.
Across `include`, `import`, and `from ... import ...`, explicit `with context` and `without context` now control scope propagation consistently; only the default mode differs by construct.
acceptance_criteria: Given a value available at the current template call site, when another template is rendered through `include` with context sharing enabled, the included template should be able to resolve that value.

Given a value available at the current template call site, when a template is imported using `{% import ... with context %}` or `{% from ... import ... with context %}`, exported macros or imported callables from that template should be able to resolve that value when used.

Given a value that exists only in the caller's active runtime scope, when `include`, `import`, or `from ... import ...` is used with `without context`, the target template or imported macro should not observe that caller-local value.

When the same template interaction is expressed via `include`, `import`, and `from ... import ...`, explicit `with context` and explicit `without context` should produce aligned scope visibility outcomes regardless of construct.
Templates that rely on the default behavior should continue to see `include` share context by default and `import` or `from ... import ...` remain isolated by default.

task_22.title: Fix sandbox handling of async generator attributes
task_22.description: The upgrade fixes a sandbox runtime bug triggered by attribute access on async generator objects. After the update, async generator attributes are evaluated under the normal sandbox safety rules instead of causing an unexpected runtime failure.

synthesized_requirement.problem_statement: Ensure that accessing attributes of async generator objects in the sandbox does not raise an unexpected runtime error and instead follows the sandbox's normal attribute-safety behavior.

expectation.grounded: Sandbox attribute classification through `is_internal_attribute(obj, attr)` must correctly handle `types.AsyncGeneratorType` instances. When an async generator attribute name is present in `UNSAFE_ASYNC_GENERATOR_ATTRIBUTES`, the sandbox should treat it as internal and unsafe; otherwise, it should continue through the existing sandbox rules without crashing.
expectation.conceptual: When sandboxed code inspects an async generator, attribute access should behave like other supported object types: unsafe async-generator attributes remain blocked by the sandbox, and supported attributes are processed normally without an unexpected runtime exception.

constraints.grounded: The change must preserve the sandbox's existing internal-attribute checks for coroutine objects, double-underscore attributes, and async generator unsafe-attribute filtering. The fix must not weaken the unsafe handling for attributes covered by `UNSAFE_ASYNC_GENERATOR_ATTRIBUTES`.
constraints.conceptual: The fix should remove the crash without broadening sandbox access. Existing security boundaries for unsafe attributes and internal attributes must remain intact.

behavior: Sandbox attribute checks no longer fail unexpectedly when the target object is an async generator.
Async generator attributes listed as unsafe continue to be classified as internal and denied by the sandbox.
Async generator attributes not covered by the sandbox's unsafe-attribute rules are evaluated under the normal sandbox attribute-access flow.
Existing handling for other protected attribute categories remains unchanged.
acceptance_criteria: When sandboxed code accesses an attribute on an async generator object, it should not terminate with an unexpected runtime error from the sandbox's internal attribute check.
When the accessed async generator attribute is one the sandbox marks as unsafe, the sandbox should treat that attribute as blocked.
When the accessed async generator attribute is not marked unsafe, the sandbox should continue normal attribute-access evaluation rather than failing during classification.
When checking coroutine or double-underscore attributes, the sandbox should retain the same protection behavior as before.
